# Rank AI — Image Hosting Architecture

**Last updated:** 2026-05-09
**Scope:** Image storage and delivery for blog posts generated by Rank AI for client websites.
**Status:** Architectural decision, locked in before skill build.

---

## Context

Rank AI is a productized service that builds client websites (Astro on Cloudflare) and posts blogs regularly using Claude + Nano Banana for hero/inline imagery. The blog routine generates 1–N images per post per client, multiplied across N clients. Storing images in each client's git repo (the current restorationai.io approach) breaks fast at this scale: repo bloat, slow deploys, no CDN, no responsive variants, deploy churn on every blog post.

This doc locks in the storage + delivery model before we build the skill, so the blog routine has a single deterministic code path.

## Stack assumptions

- All client sites hosted on **Cloudflare** (Pages / Workers).
- Most clients **own their own domain**, pointed to our Cloudflare account.
- Some clients are fully hosted on a Rank AI subdomain (`{client}.rankai.io`).
- No external CMS — blog content lives in each client's Astro repo as markdown/MDX.
- Images are generated by **Nano Banana** (`@ycse/nanobanana-mcp`, Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) at blog-write time.

## Decision

**One Cloudflare R2 bucket per client, served from a per-client image subdomain on the client's own registrable domain.**

```
R2 bucket:        rankai-{client-slug}
Custom domain:    images.{client-domain}
Object key:       blog/{YYYY}/{MM}/{post-slug}/{filename}.{ext}
Public URL:       https://images.{client-domain}/blog/{YYYY}/{MM}/{post-slug}/{filename}.{ext}
```

For Rank AI-subdomain clients without their own domain:

```
Custom domain:    images.{client}.rankai.io
Public URL:       https://images.{client}.rankai.io/blog/...
```

Same code path, different DNS target.

## Why this beats `cdn.rankai.io/{client}` for client SEO

The choice was between two patterns:

1. **`images.{clientdomain}`** — per-client subdomain on the client's own domain (chosen)
2. **`cdn.rankai.io/{client-slug}`** — single shared CDN domain owned by Rank AI

Pattern 1 wins on every SEO axis that matters:

1. **Same registrable domain = same brand entity.** `images.clientdomain.com` and `clientdomain.com` are the same eTLD+1, so Google attributes image authority, brand association, and Google Images surfaces to the client. Pattern 2 looks like third-party hotlinking — image-link equity (Pinterest pins, scrapers, AI training citations, embeds) accrues to Rank AI, not the client.

2. **Google Search Console coverage.** A client verifies their root domain and all subdomains together in one property. They see image impressions, clicks, and Image Pack rankings in *their* GSC. Pattern 2 makes the client blind to image performance on their own content.

3. **Schema.org `ImageObject` cleanliness.** When `BlogPosting.image` or `Product.image` markup specifies `contentUrl`, having it on the same registrable domain as the page reinforces entity association. Mixed-domain image objects work but are a weaker signal.

4. **Hotlink resilience flows the right way.** When a third party embeds the image, the request hits the client's domain, building their referrer footprint and analytics — not ours.

5. **Brand-trust E-E-A-T signal.** View-source, network tab, share previews — all show `clientdomain.com`. No "powered by Rank AI" leak unless the client wants it.

## Why not `clientdomain.com/cdn/...` (true same-origin)?

True same-origin (proxying R2 through a path on the main domain via a Cloudflare Worker route) is *marginally* better for SEO than a subdomain because Google sees the image as a native file on the page. The SEO delta is small enough that it doesn't justify the operational overhead — a Worker route per client, paid 100+ times as we scale. Subdomain wins on simplicity.

## Per-client onboarding sequence

One-time per client, fully scriptable through the Cloudflare MCP:

1. Create R2 bucket `rankai-{client-slug}`.
2. Connect custom domain: R2 → Settings → Custom Domains → `images.{client-domain}`.
3. Cloudflare auto-issues TLS and creates the DNS record (works because client's domain is on our Cloudflare).
4. Bucket is now publicly served at `https://images.{client-domain}/...`.
5. Store the bucket name + image base URL in the client's Rank AI config record.

Estimated wall time per client: ~2 minutes via API, faster than via dashboard.

## Blog routine — image flow

1. Nano Banana generates image bytes (PNG).
2. Routine derives object key: `blog/{YYYY}/{MM}/{post-slug}/hero.png` (or `inline-1.png`, `og.png`, etc.).
3. Routine uploads to `rankai-{client-slug}` R2 bucket via Cloudflare MCP `r2_put_object`.
4. Routine writes the public URL into the Astro markdown frontmatter (`image:` / `heroImage:`).
5. Astro build references the URL — no asset is ever copied into the client's repo.

Result: client repo stays small, deploys stay fast, all image traffic flows through Cloudflare's CDN, image transformations available for free responsive variants.

## Model selection — Flash vs Pro

The MCP package (`@ycse/nanobanana-mcp@1.1.1`) exposes a `model` parameter on `gemini_generate_image` and `gemini_edit_image`, accepting `"flash"` or `"pro"`. Under the hood:

| Param    | Model name                          | Display name      |
| -------- | ----------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| `flash`  | `gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview`    | Nano Banana 2     |
| `pro`    | `gemini-3-pro-image-preview`        | Nano Banana Pro   |

### Tradeoffs

| Dimension                  | Flash (Nano Banana 2)             | Pro (Nano Banana Pro)              |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Cost per image             | Cheaper                           | Meaningfully higher                |
| Latency                    | Few seconds                       | Slower                             |
| Prompt adherence           | Good for simple/clear prompts     | Best for complex compositions      |
| Text rendering in image    | Often imperfect                   | Much improved (still not perfect)  |
| Brand-consistency runs     | Acceptable                        | More reliable                      |
| Fine detail / realism      | Good                              | Noticeably better                  |
| Best fit                   | Volume / inline                   | Hero / social / brand assets       |

Exact pricing isn't pinned here on purpose — Google adjusts it during preview. Always reference the **AI Studio dashboard** before locking budget assumptions, and re-validate quarterly.

### Per-image-type assignment (default policy)

This is the rule the blog routine follows unless overridden by client config:

| Image role in a blog post                                       | Default model |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- |
| `heroImage` (top of post, also drives Twitter Card / OG fallback) | **Pro**       |
| `ogImage` (1200×630 social card, dedicated)                     | **Pro**       |
| Inline body images (illustrations, supporting visuals)          | **Flash**     |
| Diagrams / explanatory graphics where text rendering matters    | **Pro**       |
| Iteration / variant of an existing image (`gemini_edit_image`)  | Match the source's tier |

Reasoning: hero and OG images are the highest-leverage assets per post — they decide click-through from social, search, and AI Overviews. Spending Pro pricing on the *one* image per post that drives every share is justified; spending it on inline decorative images is not.

### Per-client override

Future config in the Rank AI control plane should support a per-client model policy, e.g.:

```toml
[clients.acme-plumbing]
image_model_policy = "pro_hero_flash_inline"   # default

[clients.premium-client]
image_model_policy = "pro_all"                 # everything Pro

[clients.budget-tier]
image_model_policy = "flash_all"               # everything Flash
```

Three policies cover ~all real cases. Don't add per-image-role fine-tuning until a client actually asks.

### Cost guardrails

Build into the skill, not learned the hard way:

1. **Per-post ceiling.** Reject (or downgrade to Flash) if a single blog post would exceed N images of Pro. Recommended initial cap: 1 hero + 1 OG + 4 inline (Flash) = 2 Pro + 4 Flash per post.
2. **Per-client daily ceiling.** Surface a warning (Slack, email, log) when a client crosses a daily image-gen spend threshold. Tunable per client.
3. **Retry budget.** If `gemini_edit_image` is iterating on a hero, cap iterations at 3. Bad prompt → log and stop, don't loop on Pro spend.
4. **Model auto-downgrade on rate limit.** If Pro returns a quota error, auto-retry once on Flash and tag the asset for human review later. Better to ship Flash than fail the post.

### What the routine actually does

```python
# pseudo-code for the blog routine's image step
def generate_image(role: str, prompt: str, client_policy: str) -> str:
    model = pick_model(role, client_policy)         # "flash" or "pro"
    img_bytes = nanobanana.generate(prompt, model=model)
    key = build_object_key(role, post_slug, ext)
    url = r2.put(bucket=f"rankai-{client_slug}", key=key, body=img_bytes)
    return url                                       # written into Astro frontmatter
```

`pick_model(role, policy)` is the single function that encodes the policy table above. Centralizing it means changing image-cost strategy is a one-file edit, not a routine-wide refactor.

## Bucket-naming convention

```
rankai-{client-slug}
```

Where `{client-slug}` is:
- lowercase
- hyphenated
- derived from the client's primary domain (strip TLD): `acmeplumbing.com` → `acmeplumbing`
- max 32 chars (R2 bucket name limit is 63, but keep headroom for prefixes)
- if collision, append `-2`, `-3`, etc.

## Object-key convention

```
blog/{YYYY}/{MM}/{post-slug}/{filename}.{ext}
```

- `{YYYY}/{MM}` = post publish date, gives natural sharding for cleanup/audits
- `{post-slug}` = matches the Astro post slug exactly, for traceability
- `{filename}` = `hero`, `og`, `inline-1`, `inline-2`, etc.
- `{ext}` = `png` from Nano Banana; convert to `webp`/`avif` at delivery time via Cloudflare Image Transformations rather than at upload (preserves lossless source)

## Image transformations

Cloudflare's built-in Image Transformations (or Image Resizing in Workers) handle responsive variants on demand:

```
https://images.clientdomain.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=800,format=auto/blog/2026/05/post-slug/hero.png
```

This means we upload one canonical PNG and serve any size/format. No build-time variant generation, no `srcset` pre-baking.

## What this removes from the blog skill

By committing to this architecture before building, the skill never has to:

- Decide where images go (always R2 per-client).
- Generate responsive variants (Cloudflare does it on request).
- Embed image bytes into markdown.
- Touch the client's repo for image assets.
- Handle hot-reload after image generation (URL is stable from the moment of upload).

The skill's image step is reduced to: generate → upload → return URL → write to frontmatter.

## Open implementation questions (resolve before skill build)

1. **R2 access pattern from the skill** — direct via Cloudflare MCP `r2_put_object`, or through a thin Worker that handles uploads? MCP direct is simpler; Worker adds auditability and rate-limiting if needed later.
2. **Image deduplication** — should we content-hash filenames to avoid re-generating identical images? Probably not worth it given Nano Banana outputs are non-deterministic.
3. **Client-config storage** — where does `{client-slug}` → R2 bucket mapping live? Likely a JSON/TOML in the Rank AI control repo, or a KV namespace.
4. **Image cleanup on post deletion** — when a blog post is unpublished or deleted, should we delete the R2 objects? Recommend keeping (cheap) and adding a quarterly orphan-sweep instead.
5. **OG / social variants** — separate object (`og.png` at 1200×630) generated alongside `hero.png`, or transformed on the fly from `hero.png` via Cloudflare? On-the-fly is simpler if hero compositions translate well to 1200×630; otherwise generate two.

## Default to lock in

Make the architecture a hard convention: **every Rank AI client gets `images.{their-domain}` provisioned on day one of onboarding, before any blog post runs.** That way the blog routine never makes a "where do images go" decision — the upload step always writes to `rankai-{client-slug}` and references `https://images.{client-domain}/blog/...`. Single code path.
